channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] FBI seizes the Chinese state-sponsored scanning and relay platforms that had been mapping US critical infrastructure
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of two linked platforms, QScan and QTRouter, operated by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and ties to a Nanjing contractor. QScan was the reconnaissance side; QTRouter relayed traffic through compromised third-party routers and IoT devices so intrusions appeared to originate from ordinary domestic addresses. Because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware for command and authentication, both platforms are now inoperable. Named victims are federal — NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy and others — and activity dates to at least 2018. For an electricity operator the takeaway is the relay layer: the source addresses in your firewall logs were never a reliable signal of who was on the other end. - US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI - Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

item.title: [Critical] UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and the affected site sat below the regulated reporting threshold
item.category: Incident — Confirmed cyberattack on a generating asset
item.description: The UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has confirmed on the record that a cyber incident affected a small-scale energy generator, while stating the wider energy system was never at risk. It is the first publicly acknowledged cyberattack on a British generating asset. The four-day outage figure and the attribution to Iran-linked actors come from Sunday Telegraph sourcing rather than an official statement, and the NCSC declined to comment. No plant, operator, technology or access route has been published. The operationally significant detail is that the NCSC logged no outage reports from regulated power station operators, which places the affected site beneath the reporting regime — and the embedded generation, CHP, standby and storage estate is numerous, frequently unmanned, and commonly reached through vendor remote access. - On-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, reported via SecurityWeek, The Record and Help Net Security; duration and attribution from the Sunday Telegraph - Telegraph report 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement 23 Aug 2026; international pickup 24 Aug 2026; incident reported as occurring in July 2026

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska: an attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from a wind farm into a heating plant and stopped its turbine
item.category: Incident — Lateral movement between unrelated operators
item.description: CERT Polska’s follow-up report describes an intrusion that began at a wind farm and ended at an unrelated combined heat and power plant, with the turbine taken out of service. The bridge was a private APN both operators bought from the same carrier. A private APN is a billing and addressing construct, not a security boundary: if devices on it can address one another, one operator’s compromised cellular router becomes another operator’s ingress path. For anyone running distributed generation over carrier links — wind, solar, storage, district energy, remote substations — this is the clearest published example of an attack path most operators have never asked their carrier about. - CERT Polska incident follow-up report — via Help Net Security, BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska disclosure 8 Aug 2026; press analysis 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Treasury sanctions an Iranian intelligence-directed network it says has been exfiltrating data from US energy companies since 2023
item.category: Incident — Nation-state targeting of energy companies
item.description: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels; the State Department posted a related reward notice. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. Read the scope carefully. What is attributed here is espionage and data theft — engineering drawings, network documentation, credentials, personnel records — not manipulation of generation or transmission equipment. The reason a utility should still care is conversion: access collected for espionage becomes disruption capability the moment tasking changes, and the vendor accounts and remote-management paths described here are the same ones a disruptive operator would inherit. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; State Department Rewards for Justice notice; reported via The Record, Nextgov/FCW and The Hacker News - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; related DOJ indictments the preceding week; press analysis 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Clop has named more than 40 victims of a PTC Windchill campaign, and what it took is engineering documentation
item.category: Incident — Supply-chain data theft affecting engineering records
item.description: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations as victims of a campaign against PTC Windchill product lifecycle management deployments, with manufacturing, aerospace and industrial suppliers among the confirmed names. Windchill holds design files, bills of material, supplier documentation and change history — the records that describe how equipment is built and configured. For a generation or transmission operator the exposure is usually indirect but real: your turbine, transformer, protection relay and balance-of-plant suppliers keep your specifications, site drawings and as-built configuration in systems like this. Ask the question of your suppliers now rather than reading your own site details on a leak site later. - Clop leak-site listings analysed by security researchers, with PTC vendor guidance — via Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek - Victim listings expanded 15 Aug 2026; PTC guidance issued earlier in August; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers across the energy sector
item.category: Threat intel — Joint federal advisory on ICS protocol tooling
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A from NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA describes actors using AI assistance to turn a well-documented open-source S7 library into custom tooling that queries internet-exposed Siemens S7 controllers and blends in as legitimate monitoring traffic. The agencies assess the activity as reconnaissance and pre-positioning rather than manipulation, and they name energy among the targeted sectors. The significant claim is not a new exploit — it is that protocol-level expertise is no longer the barrier it was. Familiarity with S7comm, DNP3 or IEC 61850 used to gate who could write working ICS tooling; it no longer does, and the population of people able to interrogate an exposed controller has grown accordingly. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A — via CISA, BleepingComputer and Industrial Cyber - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026; builds on AA26-097A from April 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA ran the same attack against two critical-infrastructure organisations — one caught it, the other never noticed
item.category: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings
item.description: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes the results of red-team assessments at a water and wastewater entity and a government organisation, run with comparable tradecraft. One organisation detected and responded; the other did not notice a domain compromise. The report is unusually direct about why. The difference was not tooling budget — both had capable products deployed — but whether anyone was reviewing what those products produced, whether identity events were correlated, and whether the team had practised the response. For a utility running an EMS or SCADA domain alongside a corporate one, the transferable finding is that Active Directory abuse and living-off-the-land movement generated telemetry in both cases; only one organisation acted on it. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter — and not one attacker needed to touch a control system
item.category: Threat intel — Quarterly industrial ransomware analysis
item.description: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up roughly 12 percent on the first, and made a point worth repeating to anyone who scopes OT security around the control system alone: operators do not need control-system access to interrupt output. Encrypting the systems that schedule, dispatch, bill and supply is enough to stop work. The utility analogue is outage management, work management, GIS, metering and settlement rather than the EMS itself — systems that carry real operational dependency but rarely receive the same segmentation, backup validation or restoration testing as the control estate. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Dragos and Help Net Security - Report covers Q2 2026; published and reported 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A seven-year-old SQL Server flaw is now confirmed exploited — and it is the database under your historian
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, historian and MES databases
item.description: CISA added six vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, and the one that matters most on the plant floor is CVE-2019-1068, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft SQL Server patched in July 2019 and only now confirmed as exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation runs code under the SQL Server Database Engine service account; where that account is over-privileged — which is common on systems installed by an integrator years ago — the attacker moves off the database and onto the Windows host. In a utility the exposure sits in the historian and the reporting tier behind the EMS or DMS — PI interfaces, outage-management reporting, relay event archives and metering data warehouses are commonly backed by a SQL Server instance an integrator built years ago and no one has revisited, and it usually lives in the corporate-facing part of the environment rather than deep in the substation network. No public write-up of the in-the-wild technique has appeared, so detection guidance is thin; the federal remediation deadline is 29 August. Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 was added in the same batch. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 — corroborated by The Hacker News and Infosecurity Magazine - Added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; original Microsoft patch July 2019; federal remediation deadline 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from “patch soon” to confirmed in-the-wild exploitation. The flaw is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August, following publication of a technical analysis and proof of concept. Federal agencies must remediate by 29 August. For utilities, NetScaler frequently fronts the remote access that engineering, control-centre and vendor staff use to reach OT. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis - Vendor advisory and patches released August 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Two unauthenticated flaws in Veeam ONE 13 — the monitoring layer that watches the backups you would restore from
item.category: Advisory — Backup and monitoring infrastructure, unauthenticated
item.description: Veeam disclosed vulnerabilities in Veeam ONE 13 in knowledge-base articles published on 25 August. CVE-2026-64633 is rated CVSS v4.0 10.0 and allows remote, unauthenticated code execution on the Veeam ONE agent host; CVE-2026-65641 is rated 9.3 and lets a remote unauthenticated attacker coerce SMB authentication out of the Veeam ONE service account, which is the first step in relaying that account somewhere more useful. Veeam ONE 13.x is affected and the 12.x line is not. On the grid side Veeam ONE is typically the console watching backups of the EMS, historian and substation engineering workstations — the recovery capability you would need if a control-centre application had to be rebuilt. There is no report of exploitation yet, but backup and monitoring servers are a standing target precisely because compromising them removes the recovery option before the ransomware runs. - Veeam knowledge-base articles KB4905 and KB4892 — corroborated by CyberScoop and Cybersecurity News - Vendor advisory published 25 Aug 2026; patched builds available the same day

item.title: [Critical] The Git server holding your PLC projects just went into KEV — Gitea is being exploited without much effort
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, engineering toolchain
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the KEV catalogue on 25 August after reports of active exploitation. The flaw, rated CVSS 9.8, lets anyone with ordinary repository write access plant an executable Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Gitea 1.27.1 fixed it on 27 July; exploitation followed within a month. Self-hosted Gitea has quietly become common in engineering groups because it is easy to stand up inside a plant network for PLC projects, HMI screens, configuration baselines and automation scripts. That is precisely the problem: a modest contractor account becomes code execution on a server that holds the authoritative copy of your control logic. Federal remediation was due 28 August. - CISA KEV catalogue addition — corroborated by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Gitea 1.27.1 released 27 Jul 2026; advisory 28 Jul; added to KEV 25 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway — the management interface takes commands from anyone who can reach it
item.category: Advisory — Maximum severity, Siemens edge gateway
item.description: Siemens’ August advisory set includes a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices, where the management interface allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute code with elevated privileges. Ten Siemens advisories landed in the same batch alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact publications. The IoT2050 matters disproportionately in generation and substation environments because of where it sits: these gateways are deployed specifically to bridge process data out to historians, analytics platforms and cloud services, which means they are dual-homed by design and frequently the one device with a route in both directions. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories and the CISA ICS advisory batch — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] No login required and no patch coming — the Ebyte gateway advisory is a replacement decision
item.category: Advisory — Serial-to-Ethernet gateway, no vendor patch
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-06 covers the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, where the web management interface does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative functionality. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read configuration, change device settings, hijack sessions or disrupt operation. CISA notes the vendor acknowledged the reports and said a patch was in development, then stopped responding — so no fix status is available. Low-cost serial gateways like this turn up in generation and substation environments wherever an older meter, relay or protection device needed to reach an Ethernet network, and they are rarely in anyone’s patch programme. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-237-06, reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA - Published 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 27 Aug 2026 — no vendor patch announced

item.title: [High] A hard-coded key in Johnson Controls Airwall — the product many sites use to protect everything else
item.category: Advisory — Hard-coded key in a segmentation product
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-03 republishes a Johnson Controls advisory covering a hard-coded cryptographic key in Airwall, alongside an arbitrary file read issue. Airwall is a micro-segmentation and secure-remote-access product; utilities and their integrators deploy it specifically to isolate substation, plant and building-systems networks and to broker vendor access. A weakness in a compensating control is worth more attention than the same weakness in an ordinary application, because the architecture diagram assumes this device holds. Where Airwall is the boundary between a corporate network and a substation or plant LAN, the patch is not a routine item. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-03, republishing the Johnson Controls advisory — via CISA - Published 13 Aug 2026 in CISA’s mid-August advisory batch; re-verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A new executive order puts foreign-made grid equipment — including RTUs and control systems — under federal review
item.category: Policy — Supply chain, bulk-power system equipment
item.description: Executive Order 14420, signed 26 August, prohibits the acquisition, importation, transfer or installation of certain foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment and directs the Department of Energy to restrict, condition or unwind equipment it judges to carry sabotage, cyber, supply-disruption or catastrophic-infrastructure risk. The order is grounded in a declared national emergency over the possibility of digital backdoors built into foreign-manufactured equipment that would permit remote access and sabotage. What makes it operationally significant rather than purely political is the scope: alongside transformers, inverters and energy storage, it names industrial control systems explicitly, including remote terminal units. Countries named in reporting on the order include China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. Implementation detail, including how existing installed equipment will be treated, sits with DOE and has not yet been published. - Executive Order 14420, signed 26 Aug 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Executive order signed and reported 26 Aug 2026; Department of Energy implementing criteria not yet published

item.title: [Info] The NSA is putting an ISA/IEC 62443 certificate in front of the controllers it buys — and the pattern will not stay inside government
item.description: ISASecure announced a partnership with the National Security Agency to develop a High Criticality Component Security Assurance certification scheme, derived from its existing Component Security Assurance programme and grounded in ISA/IEC 62443-4-2. Once complete and accepted, the NSA intends to use it as an approved mechanism for adding OT components to the National Security Systems product compliant list. The reason this matters beyond government procurement is precedent: when a large buyer makes a certification a condition of purchase, vendors build to it, and the resulting requirement language propagates into the specifications everyone else writes. Utilities drafting procurement standards now have a reference point worth citing. - ISA / ISASecure press release — corroborated by Automation World and ISSSource - Announced 20 Aug 2026; verified 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The 2026 CIP picture: CIP-003-9 and CIP-012-2 now in force, CIP-015 internal monitoring ahead
item.description: Three dates define this year for registered entities. CIP-003-9 became enforceable on 1 April 2026, extending governance expectations to low-impact BES cyber systems with particular attention to vendor remote access and supply chain. CIP-012-2 took effect on 1 July 2026, tightening protection of real-time operational data exchanged between control centres. CIP-015-1 has been effective since September 2025 with phased compliance running to 2030, and introduces internal network security monitoring — east-west visibility inside the electronic security perimeter rather than only at its edge. NERC’s January 2026 CIP roadmap signals where the standards go next, including cloud, telecommunications dependency and inverter-based resources. - NERC standards and the January 2026 CIP roadmap — summarised via Ampyx Cyber and Certrec - CIP-015-1 effective 2 Sep 2025; CIP-003-9 enforceable 1 Apr 2026; CIP-012-2 effective 1 Jul 2026; roadmap published Jan 2026; status verified 27 Aug 2026
